claims.text: Adding 1–3 at.% of a refractory element to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will improve its glass-forming ability.
Adding 1–3 at.% of a refractory element will enhance the thermal stability of the alloy's amorphous state.
Niobium is a suitable refractory microalloying element for the proposed intervention.
The intervention should operate under conventional melt-quenching or rapid-solidification conditions.
Significant phosphorus content is required for the proposed benefit.
Keeping the refractory addition at a minor concentration helps avoid phase separation or unwanted crystallization.
The refractory element tends to form localized, stable clusters in the alloy.
Localized refractory-element clusters enhance local atomic packing.
The refractory addition disrupts sites at which crystallization nuclei would otherwise form.
The refractory addition promotes short-range atomic order.
The refractory addition impedes atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility and altered short-range order raise the crystallization onset temperature.
Reduced atomic mobility and altered short-range order lower the critical cooling rate required for glass formation.
Relative to an otherwise identical alloy without the refractory addition, the modified alloy will have a significantly lower critical cooling rate.
Relative to an otherwise identical alloy without the refractory addition, the modified alloy will have a higher crystallization onset temperature.
The benefit may diminish or reverse above a critical refractory-element concentration.
Cooling rates that are too slow may prevent the proposed beneficial atomic-packing effects from manifesting.
The magnitude of the improvement depends on the specific alloy system and processing conditions.
